ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A behavioral endocrinologist captures male individuals of a territorial bird species over the course of a year to measure testosterone (T) levels. In this population, males may play one of two roles: (1) they may stay in their natal group (the group they were born in) and help raise their younger siblings, or (2) they may leave the natal group to establish a new territory. Use this information and the two histograms that follow to answer the following questions.

What can you infer about the role of testosterone in reproduction in this species?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The first histogram is labeled “Non-breeding season.” It shows mean testosterone level for helper males and breeding males, and both bars are low and approximately equal, around 10. The second histogram is labeled “Breeding season.” It shows helper males still at a low mean testosterone level around 10, while breeding males have a much higher mean testosterone level, around 50. Reasoning: During the breeding season, only the males in the breeding role show elevated testosterone, while helper males remain low. Since breeding males are the individuals that leave to establish territories for reproduction, the high testosterone level is associated with the reproductive role rather than simply being male or seasonal. Therefore, testosterone appears to promote or aid breeding in this species.
